---
title: "The same logistic models in R, statsmodels and PHP"
jupyter: python3
---

We fit the same saved observations and design columns in all three runtimes.
See the [math walkthrough](logistic-math.qmd) for how likelihood, Newton updates
and normal Wald inference produce these quantities.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import sys
import pandas as pd
ROOT = next(p for p in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents] if (p / "Cargo.toml").exists())
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT / "docs/verifications"))
from compare_logistic import cases, compare_case
results = [compare_case(case) for case in cases()]
first = results[0]
print(first["versions"])
rows = []
for implementation in ["R", "statsmodels", "phit"]:
    fit = first[implementation]
    for j, label in enumerate(["intercept", "study hours", "practice score"]):
        rows.append({"implementation": implementation, "coefficient": label,
                     "estimate": fit["coefficients"][j], "SE": fit["std_errors"][j],
                     "z": fit["z_statistics"][j], "p": fit["p_values"][j],
                     "95% lower": fit["conf_int"][j][0], "95% upper": fit["conf_int"][j][1]})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows))
display(pd.DataFrame([{ "case": r["name"], "retained n": r["phit"]["n_observations"],
                        "iterations (PHP)": r["phit"]["iterations"],
                        "max absolute difference vs R": max(e for values in r["max_absolute_errors_vs_R"].values() for e in values.values()),
                        "warnings": len(r["warnings"])} for r in results]))
```

All complete statistical outputs, including every fitted probability and residual,
are checked at tolerance 1e-9 + 1e-7 × abs(reference). Differences in iteration
counts are expected because initial values and convergence rules differ.

## Equivalent calls

R adds an intercept in this formula; the reference runners pass the same explicit
design to Python and PHP (`intercept: false` in PHP). Application calls can
instead supply predictors only and use the automatic fixed intercept.

```r
students <- read.csv("docs/data/learning.csv")
fit <- glm(passed ~ study_hours + practice_score, data=students,
           family=binomial(), control=glm.control(epsilon=1e-14, maxit=100))
coef(fit)
vcov(fit)
confint.default(fit) # normal Wald, not profile likelihood
```

```python
students = pd.read_csv("docs/data/learning.csv")
x = sm.add_constant(students[["study_hours", "practice_score"]])
fit = sm.Logit(students["passed"], x).fit(method="newton", tol=1e-10, maxiter=100)
fit.params, fit.bse, fit.conf_int()
```

```php
$x = []; $y = [];
foreach ($students as $student) {
    $x[] = [
        1.0,
        $student['study_hours'],
        $student['practice_score'],
    ];
    $y[] = $student['passed'];
}
$result = Phit\fit_logistic_matrix(
    x: $x,
    y: $y,
    intercept: false,
);
```

Here `$students` holds numeric records; `examples/logistic.php` has the complete CSV
conversion. This comparison builds the design explicitly so all three
implementations receive identical columns, and `intercept: false` stops phit
adding a second intercept. Applications can use the formula interface instead:
see [Linear and generalized linear models](../models.qmd).

## Missing rows and model statistics

```{python}
missing = results[-1]
print("Retained rows:", missing["phit"]["retained_rows"])
print("Dropped rows:", missing["phit"]["dropped_rows"])
print("PHP warnings:", missing["warnings"])
display(pd.DataFrame([{ "implementation": name,
                       **{key: first[name][key] for key in ["log_likelihood", "deviance", "null_deviance", "aic", "df_residual"]}}
                      for name in ["R", "statsmodels", "phit"]]))
```

The runner applies the identical retained sample before fitting reference models.
For no-intercept cases it explicitly calculates the fixed 0.5 null baseline,
rather than using statsmodels' intercept-only null fit. Deviance uses individual
Bernoulli outcomes, and no Gaussian residual variance is estimated. See the
[verification record](../verifications/logistic.qmd) for rejection cases and limits.
